title: The Quiet Reinvention of Assessment
author: Hardman, Philippa
summary: Dr. Philippa Hardman surveys how AI has forced a wholesale rethinking of assessment in both higher education and corporate L&D; settings by 2026. The initial defensive response—AI bans, detection tools, a return to in-person exams—has given way to a more substantive reinvention: educators and learning designers are now building assessment practices that AI cannot simply do for the learner, because they require live demonstration, contextual judgment, and real-world performance. Hardman catalogs emerging assessment modalities including portfolio-based learning, authentic performance tasks, oral defense formats, and continuous low-stakes assessment with human feedback. The article argues that the real gift of AI-induced disruption is the forced abandonment of assessments that were really only measuring compliance (Did the student do the task?) rather than capability (Can the student perform?). The shift toward performance-based assessment is, in Hardman's view, long overdue and now becoming irreversible.
points: AI broke the old assessment model by making compliance-based assignments trivially completable: any task that could be done without being present—without applying judgment to a specific context—can now be done by AI.

The defensive phase (detection tools, bans) has largely failed: AI detection is unreliable, in-person exams are logistically expensive, and neither addresses the deeper question of what assessment is for.

Performance-based assessment is the durable response: oral defenses, live demonstrations, portfolio reviews, and real-world task completion require the learner to be present and capable, not just submissive.

Corporate L&D; was already moving in this direction but AI has accelerated it dramatically: organizations care about on-the-job performance, and assessment that doesn't predict performance is a sunk cost.
The AI disruption may ultimately improve assessment practice: by forcing abandonment of compliance-as-assessment, educators are building systems that actually measure what they claim to measure.
quotes: Two years ago we acknowledged AI had broken assessment. Initially, the reaction was defensive. In higher education, AI bans, huge investment in AI detection tools and a return to in-person examination were standard in 2024.
Meanwhile, in corporate L&D;, many of us worried that employees were quietly outsourcing their learning to AI—going through the motions of assessment without actually developing the capability.
The real problem with most assessments was not that AI could do them—it was that they were never really measuring what we said they were measuring in the first place.
Performance-based assessment requires the learner to be present. You cannot delegate presence. You cannot outsource judgment. You cannot submit a live demonstration.
What AI has done is reveal the gap between assessment-as-compliance and assessment-as-evidence-of-capability. The gap was always there. Now it is impossible to ignore.
